stem: A regional consulting firm advises pension plans on manager selection and also licenses portfolio accounting software to asset managers. Neither activity involves managing assets for clients. Regarding a claim of compliance with the GIPS standards, the firm most likely:
options: may claim compliance, provided its calculations follow GIPS methodology
may not claim compliance, because the firm does not manage any client assets
may claim compliance, provided an independent verifier reviews the reported figures
distractor_reason: Treats correct calculation methodology as the criterion for eligibility to claim compliance.
Assumes verification can confer eligibility on an entity that falls outside the scope of the standards.
hint: Consider which kind of entity the standards were written to govern.
explanation: The GIPS standards apply to firms that actually manage assets, so consultants, plan sponsors and software vendors fall outside their scope and cannot claim compliance. Correct methodology and independent review do not extend eligibility to an entity that manages no client money. Had the firm operated a discretionary asset management business, it could have claimed compliance for that business on a firm-wide basis.

stem: A fund management company in Ho Chi Minh City reports results for its domestic equity composite in line with the GIPS standards, while its balanced and fixed income composites follow the firm's own internal methodology. Regarding the firm's position, the most accurate statement is that compliance:
options: is claimed on a firm-wide basis, so the other composites must also comply
is claimed for each composite, so the domestic equity composite qualifies alone
is claimed once the majority of a firm's composites meet the requirements
distractor_reason: Treats compliance as something that can be asserted for a single composite in isolation.
Assumes partial coverage across a firm's composites can support a claim of compliance.
hint: Consider the unit to which a claim of compliance attaches.
explanation: A claim of compliance with the GIPS standards is made by the firm as a whole, not composite by composite, so every composite the firm manages must be constructed and reported in line with the requirements. Running one composite to GIPS methodology while others follow internal rules therefore does not support a claim. Had the firm applied the requirements across all its composites, the claim would have been available.

stem: An investment firm groups portfolios for performance reporting and its head of performance is asked how a composite should be understood. Under the GIPS standards, a composite is most accurately described as:
options: an aggregation of portfolios assigned to one manager within the firm
an asset-weighted average of returns across a firm's similar portfolios
an aggregation of portfolios managed to a similar mandate or objective
distractor_reason: Confuses the manager responsible for a group of portfolios with the strategy that defines a composite.
Treats the composite return figure as the definition of the composite itself.
hint: Consider what has to be shared by the portfolios that sit together in one group.
explanation: A composite under the GIPS standards is an aggregation of one or more portfolios managed according to a similar investment mandate, objective or strategy. The defining feature is the shared mandate, not the identity of the manager, and the composite is the group of portfolios rather than the return figure calculated from them. A firm organised so that one manager runs several distinct strategies would have several composites, not one.

stem: At the end of a reporting year a Bangkok asset manager reviews its emerging markets composite and removes two portfolios whose results were unusually weak, on the grounds that their mandates were slightly unusual. The mandates had not been documented as exclusions. Regarding composite construction, the firm most likely:
options: acted properly, because portfolios with unusual mandates fall outside the composite
breached the requirements, because inclusion must rest on pre-established criteria
acted properly, because year-end review is when composites are finalised
distractor_reason: Treats a characteristic noticed after the results are known as a valid ground for exclusion.
Assumes composite membership can be settled retrospectively once performance is visible.
hint: Consider when the rules for admitting a portfolio to a group have to be fixed.
explanation: The GIPS standards require portfolios to be assigned to composites on the basis of criteria established in advance, so that a firm cannot select which results to present once performance is known. Removing weak portfolios at year-end on grounds never documented is exactly the survivorship problem the standards were written to prevent. Had the firm defined and recorded the unusual mandates as a separate composite before the period began, excluding them would have been acceptable.

stem: A fund management company in Hanoi presents five years of composite returns to a prospective client. The returns are shown net of investment management fees, but the presentation does not state whether fees have been deducted. Regarding required disclosures, the presentation most likely:
options: falls short, because the treatment of fees must be disclosed in the presentation
meets the requirements, because net returns are the more conservative figure
meets the requirements, because the client can request the fee schedule separately
distractor_reason: Assumes a conservative presentation removes the need to state how the figures were computed.
Treats information available on request as equivalent to disclosure within the presentation.
hint: Consider what a reader needs to be told in order to interpret a return figure correctly.
explanation: The GIPS standards require a compliant presentation to disclose whether returns are shown gross or net of fees, because the same figure carries a different meaning under each treatment. Showing net returns without saying so leaves the prospective client unable to compare the record with other managers, so the presentation falls short. Had the presentation stated that returns were net of investment management fees, the requirement would have been satisfied.

stem: A securities firm's marketing team prepares a factsheet showing composite performance and adds a line stating that the figures were prepared in accordance with recognised international performance standards. Regarding the claim of compliance, this wording most likely:
options: satisfies the claim, because the reference conveys compliance in substance
satisfies the claim, because marketing material sits outside the disclosure rules
falls short, because the standards prescribe the exact wording of the claim
distractor_reason: Assumes a description capturing the general idea can replace the prescribed statement.
Treats promotional material as exempt from the presentation requirements.
hint: Consider how much latitude a firm has in how it words a claim of compliance.
explanation: The GIPS standards specify the wording a firm must use when claiming compliance, so a paraphrase that gestures at international standards does not meet the requirement. Prescribing the language protects readers, who would otherwise have to judge for themselves whether a loose phrase means full compliance. Had the factsheet carried the required compliance statement, the claim would have been properly made.

stem: A firm claiming compliance with the GIPS standards is asked by a prospective client why it has not engaged an outside verifier. Regarding verification under the standards, the most accurate response is that verification:
options: is required of any firm that wishes to claim compliance with the standards
is voluntary, and confirms the accuracy of each composite presentation shown
is voluntary, and is performed across the firm rather than on one composite
distractor_reason: Treats an optional assurance step as a precondition for claiming compliance.
Assumes verification certifies individual composite figures rather than firm-level processes.
hint: Consider both whether the step is obligatory and what it actually tests.
explanation: Verification under the GIPS standards is voluntary, and it tests whether a firm's policies and procedures for calculating and presenting performance comply with the standards on a firm-wide basis. It does not certify the accuracy of any particular composite presentation, and a firm may claim compliance without it. Had the client asked whether verification adds credibility, the firm could fairly have said that it does, without conceding that it is required.

stem: An asset management company in Singapore asks its internal audit department to review the firm's performance policies and then describes its composite presentations as verified. The internal team reports separately from the investment division. Regarding this description, the firm most likely:
options: may not use it, because verification must be performed by an outside party
may use it, because the reviewing team is independent of portfolio management
may use it, because the review covered the firm's policies and procedures
distractor_reason: Assumes internal independence can substitute for review by a party outside the firm.
Confuses the scope of what verification examines with the question of who may perform it.
hint: Consider who has to stand behind the assurance before the term may be used.
explanation: Under the GIPS standards verification must be carried out by an independent third party, so a firm cannot verify itself however well its internal audit function is separated from the investment team. Describing presentations as verified after an internal review therefore misleads the reader about the assurance obtained. Had the firm engaged an external verifier to perform the same firm-wide review, the description would have been accurate.

stem: A compliance officer is preparing training material and lists several duties for new analysts. She wants to separate the general principles of the Code of Ethics from the more specific conduct requirements. Which of the following most likely belongs to the Code of Ethics?
options: Deal fairly with all clients when disseminating investment recommendations to them
Use reasonable care and exercise independent judgement in professional activities
Disclose to clients any matter that could impair independence and objectivity
distractor_reason: Confuses a specific conduct requirement about fair dealing with a general principle of the Code.
Treats a detailed disclosure obligation as one of the Code's broad ethical principles.
hint: Distinguish the broad values a member commits to from the specific rules that follow from them.
explanation: The Code of Ethics sets out six broad principles, one of which requires members to use reasonable care and exercise independent professional judgement in investment analysis, recommendations and actions. Fair dealing in disseminating recommendations and disclosure of matters impairing independence are specific requirements found in the Standards of Professional Conduct, which set minimum benchmarks rather than principles. Had the question asked which items are Standards, the other two would have been correct.

stem: A portfolio manager is reviewing the Code of Ethics with a junior colleague, who asks how the Code ranks competing interests. Under the Code of Ethics, members and candidates commit to placing:
options: the integrity of the profession and client interests above their own
the interests of their employer above those of individual clients
client interests above the integrity of the capital markets themselves
distractor_reason: Reverses the ranking by placing the employer ahead of the client.
Treats duties to clients as overriding the obligation to market integrity.
hint: Consider whose interests the Code asks a member to subordinate.
explanation: The Code of Ethics requires members and candidates to place the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above their own personal interests. It does not subordinate clients to employers, nor does it set client interests against the integrity of the capital markets, which members also commit to promoting. A situation in which an employer's instruction conflicted with a client's interest would engage the Standards on duties to clients and to employers.

stem: A charterholder argues that her responsibility regarding professional competence runs no further than keeping her own knowledge current. Under the Code of Ethics, a member's obligation in respect of competence most likely extends to:
options: maintaining her own competence and that of the staff she directly supervises
maintaining her own competence and that of other investment professionals
maintaining her own competence to the standard her employer requires
distractor_reason: Narrows a duty owed to the profession generally down to a supervisory relationship.
Treats an employer's expectations as the measure of professional competence.
hint: Consider how far beyond the individual the competence commitment reaches.
explanation: The Code of Ethics requires members to maintain and improve their own professional competence and to strive to maintain and improve the competence of other investment professionals. The duty is owed to the profession at large, so it is not confined to direct reports and it is not measured by what an employer happens to require. Supervisory responsibilities over specific staff are addressed separately under the Standards.

stem: An analyst learns that a colleague at another firm routinely overstates his qualifications in client meetings. She takes the view that the colleague's conduct is no concern of hers. Under the Code of Ethics, her position is most likely inconsistent with the commitment to:
options: report suspected misconduct to the professional's employer
verify the qualifications of other professionals met in client meetings
encourage others to practise in an ethical and professional manner
distractor_reason: Converts a broad commitment into a specific reporting obligation the Code does not impose.
Reads the commitment as a duty to check the credentials of other market participants.
hint: Consider whether the commitment stops at the member's own conduct.
explanation: The Code of Ethics requires members to practise and to encourage others to practise in a professional and ethical manner that reflects credit on themselves and on the profession, so indifference to a colleague's conduct sits uneasily with it. The commitment is to encouragement and example rather than to a defined duty of reporting or credential checking, neither of which the Code imposes in these terms. Had the colleague been the analyst's own supervisee, Standard IV(C) would also have been engaged.

stem: A trader takes the view that his responsibilities under the Code of Ethics run to his clients and his employer, and no further. Under the Code of Ethics, members and candidates also commit to:
options: promote the integrity of the capital markets and uphold their rules
report market abuse observed at other firms to the relevant regulator
place the interests of the market ahead of those of their clients
distractor_reason: Converts a general commitment to market integrity into a specific reporting duty.
Sets market integrity against client interests, which the Code treats as complementary.
hint: Consider whether the Code's reach stops at the people a member deals with directly.
explanation: The Code of Ethics requires members and candidates to promote the integrity of, and uphold the rules governing, the capital markets, which extends their responsibilities beyond clients and employer to the market as a whole. The commitment is expressed as a general principle rather than as a duty to report particular conduct to a regulator, and it does not rank the market above clients. Specific market conduct duties appear under Standard II.

stem: A new candidate asks how the Code of Ethics differs from the Standards of Professional Conduct. The most accurate distinction is that the Code sets out:
options: minimum required behaviour, while the Standards set broad principles
general principles, while the Standards set minimum required behaviour
obligations for firms, while the Standards bind individual members and candidates
distractor_reason: Reverses the two documents, treating the Code as the detailed benchmark.
Draws the distinction by who is bound rather than by what each document does.
hint: Consider what each document is for, rather than who it applies to.
explanation: The Code of Ethics states the general principles and values that members and candidates commit to, while the Standards of Professional Conduct set the minimum acceptable behaviour expected of them. Both apply to the same population of individual members and candidates, so the difference lies in the level of generality rather than in scope of application. A firm that adopts the Code as its internal code does so voluntarily.

stem: A securities firm adopts the CFA Institute Code and Standards as its own internal code of conduct and states this in its client materials. Regarding who is bound by the Code and Standards, the most accurate statement is that they apply to:
options: individual members and candidates, and to firms adopting them internally
any professional working in the investment industry within that jurisdiction
individual members and candidates, whom firms may encourage to follow them
distractor_reason: Treats voluntary adoption by a firm as bringing the firm within the scope of the Code.
Extends the Code to a whole industry rather than to a defined membership.
hint: Consider on whom the obligation actually falls when a firm adopts the Code.
explanation: The Code and Standards apply to individual members of CFA Institute and to candidates in the CFA Program; firms are encouraged to adopt them but are not themselves bound by them. A firm's voluntary adoption creates internal expectations for its staff without making the firm subject to CFA Institute enforcement. Had an employee of the firm been a candidate, that individual would have been bound in his or her own right.

stem: A candidate enrolled in the CFA Program is told by a colleague that the Code and Standards carry no weight because they are not law. Regarding the candidate's obligation to comply, the most accurate statement is that compliance is:
options: obligatory for candidates, though it does not arise from a legal duty
recommended for candidates, since the Code operates as guidance
a legal duty for candidates in jurisdictions that recognise the designation
distractor_reason: Treats an obligatory commitment as advisory because it lacks the force of law.
Confuses an obligation owed to CFA Institute with an obligation imposed by law.
hint: Separate the question of whether compliance is required from the question of what makes it required.
explanation: Compliance with the Code and Standards is mandatory for all candidates enrolled in the CFA Program, and breaches expose a candidate to disciplinary sanction through the Professional Conduct Program. That obligation arises from enrolment rather than from law, so it is neither optional nor a legal duty. A candidate whose conduct also breached local securities law would face separate consequences under that law.

stem: Pham Ngoc Anh, CFA, works for a fund manager headquartered in Singapore and is seconded to a branch in a market whose disclosure rules for related-party transactions are less demanding than those of her home regulator. Her branch manager tells her to follow local practice, which she confirms is lawful there. Anh applies the lighter local requirement. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Anh most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because she confirmed the practice was lawful in that market
breached the Standards, because the stricter of the applicable requirements governs
acted appropriately, because a seconded employee follows the branch manager's direction
distractor_reason: Treats local legality as the ceiling of a member's obligation rather than its floor.
Allows an internal instruction to displace a requirement the member is personally subject to.
hint: Where two regimes both reach the member's conduct, ask which one sets the higher bar.
explanation: Standard I(A) requires members to comply with the most strict applicable law, rule or regulation, and where the Code and Standards impose a higher requirement than local law, to follow the Code and Standards. Confirming that lighter disclosure is lawful in the host market does not release Anh from the stricter home-regulator requirement that also reaches her conduct. Had no stricter regime applied to her, following local practice would have been correct. Standard IV(A) does not permit an employer's instruction to override this.

stem: Chua Wei Ling, CFA, discovers that a colleague has been allocating profitable trades to a favoured account. She raises the matter with her supervisor, who tells her the practice will be reviewed later. Weeks pass with no change. Chua continues to prepare the trade files that the colleague uses. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Chua most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because she continued participating after escalation failed
acted appropriately, because she escalated the matter to the proper internal channel
acted appropriately, because responsibility for the practice rests with her supervisor
distractor_reason: Treats a single act of escalation as discharging the duty however the firm responds.
Transfers a personal obligation to a supervisor by virtue of the reporting line.
hint: Consider what a member must do when an internal report produces no result.
explanation: Standard I(A) prohibits a member from knowingly participating in or assisting a violation, and requires dissociation from the activity where the conduct continues. Reporting once and then carrying on preparing the files leaves Chua contributing to the very practice she identified, so the Standard is breached. Had she stopped preparing the files and, if necessary, sought legal advice about further steps, she would have complied. Standard III(B) is also engaged, since the allocation favours one account over others.

stem: Hoang Duc Trung, CFA, joins a boutique advisory firm in Hanoi that has no compliance function. He assumes that in the absence of internal guidance he is bound only by the securities law of the jurisdiction in which he operates. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Trung's assumption is most likely:
options: incorrect, because members remain bound by the Code and Standards independently
correct, because the Code and Standards operate through the employer's compliance programme
correct, because a firm without a compliance function cannot impose further duties
distractor_reason: Treats membership obligations as reaching the member only through a firm's internal programme.
Makes the existence of a personal obligation depend on the employer's internal resources.
hint: Ask where a member's obligation under the Code and Standards comes from in the first place.
explanation: Standard I(A) binds members and candidates personally, so the obligation to understand and comply with applicable law and with the Code and Standards does not depend on an employer having a compliance function. A firm's programme may help a member meet that obligation but is not its source. Had Trung's firm maintained a compliance manual, he would still have been responsible for his own conduct under the Standards.

stem: Rattana Phueng, CFA, covers a listed logistics group for a Bangkok brokerage. The company invites her to tour a new terminal and offers to cover a two-night stay at a resort near the site, well beyond what the visit requires. She discloses the arrangement to her supervisor and to readers of her report, then accepts. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Phueng most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the benefit was disclosed to her firm and to readers
breached the Standards, because the benefit exceeds what the visit reasonably needs
acted appropriately, because a site visit improves the quality of her research coverage
distractor_reason: Treats disclosure as curing a benefit that is capable of impairing objectivity.
Uses the research value of the visit to justify hospitality unrelated to that value.
hint: Ask whether telling people about a benefit is enough when the benefit itself is the problem.
explanation: Standard I(B) requires members to use reasonable care and judgement to maintain independence and objectivity, and recommends that analysts pay for their own travel where practicable and limit any issuer-funded arrangement to what the visit requires. A resort stay beyond the needs of the tour is the kind of benefit capable of compromising objectivity, and disclosure does not neutralise it. Had the company covered only modest local transport to a site not otherwise reachable, acceptance would have been defensible.

stem: Goh Mei Fen, CFA, heads research at a Singapore investment bank. The head of corporate finance asks her to delay publication of a downgrade on a company until an underwriting mandate is decided, noting that the recommendation itself will be unchanged. Goh delays publication by three weeks. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Goh most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the substance of the recommendation remained unaltered
acted appropriately, because timing decisions sit within a research head's discretion
breached the Standards, because the delay subordinates research to banking interests
distractor_reason: Assumes objectivity is preserved so long as the conclusion itself is not rewritten.
Treats a decision within a member's authority as therefore free of independence concerns.
hint: Consider whether when a view is released can compromise independence as much as what it says.
explanation: Standard I(B) requires members to maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities, which extends to the timing of research as well as its content. Withholding a downgrade so that a banking relationship is not disturbed lets an investment banking interest shape what clients see and when, so the Standard is breached even though the rating is unchanged. Had the delay arisen from further verification work on the analysis itself, it would have been legitimate. Standard III(B) is engaged if some clients learn of the view during the delay.

stem: Ly Bao Chau, CFA, manages a manager-selection programme for an insurance company. A fund house competing for a mandate offers her a place at a professional conference it is hosting, with registration and standard economy travel paid. She reports the offer to her employer, which permits attendance under a written gifts policy. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Chau most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because any benefit from a bidder compromises her judgement
acted appropriately, because the benefit is modest and was cleared by her employer
breached the Standards, because attendance signals a preference among the bidders
distractor_reason: Treats every benefit from an interested party as disqualifying, whatever its scale.
Assumes the appearance of preference arises from attendance rather than from the decision itself.
hint: Weigh the size and nature of the benefit against the judgement it might realistically affect.
explanation: Standard I(B) does not prohibit all benefits from interested parties; it requires members to use reasonable care and judgement so that independence and objectivity are maintained. Modest, education-related attendance on standard travel terms, reported to and cleared by the employer, falls within what the Standard permits. Had the fund house offered first-class travel, extended hospitality or a personal gift, acceptance would have been inconsistent with the Standard.

stem: Doan Hai Yen passed the Level II examination in the CFA Program and is registered for Level III. Her employer's website describes her as holding an advanced qualification from CFA Institute and lists her among the firm's charterholders. Yen reviews the page and leaves it unchanged. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Yen most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because she left a false description of her status online
acted appropriately, because the website was written and published by the firm
acted appropriately, because progress to Level III is an accurate factual statement
distractor_reason: Treats authorship by the employer as removing the member's responsibility for the claim.
Confuses a true statement about examination progress with the claim actually published.
hint: Consider a member's responsibility for statements about herself that she knows are inaccurate.
explanation: Standard I(C) prohibits members and candidates from knowingly making any misrepresentation relating to their qualifications or credentials, and reviewing an inaccurate description without correcting it amounts to allowing that misrepresentation to continue. Passing Level II does not make Yen a charterholder, so the listing is false whoever drafted it. Had she asked the firm to describe her accurately as a Level III candidate, the Standard would have been satisfied. Standard VII(B) also governs how candidacy may be referenced.

stem: Tan Jun Hao, CFA, prepares a client presentation on a frontier market and incorporates several paragraphs of analysis taken from a report published by a global index provider. He names the provider in a footnote on the final page but presents the analysis in his own voice throughout. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Tan most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the source is identified within the presentation document
acted appropriately, because information from a recognised provider is publicly available
breached the Standards, because the passages are presented as his own analysis
distractor_reason: Treats a general acknowledgement as equivalent to attributing specific passages to their author.
Assumes public availability removes the obligation to credit another's work.
hint: Consider what a reader would conclude about the authorship of the passages as presented.
explanation: Standard I(C) treats plagiarism as a misrepresentation, and it requires members to acknowledge the specific material they use rather than merely to list a source somewhere in the document. Presenting another firm's paragraphs in his own voice leaves clients believing the analysis is Tan's, so the Standard is breached despite the footnote. Had he attributed the passages at the point of use, or summarised them with clear credit, he would have complied.

stem: Bui Quang Huy, CFA, is a fixed income trader. Away from work he is convicted of falsifying documents in a dispute over a family property, and the conviction is reported in the local press. His employer takes no action, noting that the matter had nothing to do with his trading duties. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Huy most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because dishonesty reflects on his professional integrity
did not breach, because the conduct arose outside his professional duties
did not breach, because his employer concluded that his trading role was unaffected
distractor_reason: Assumes conduct outside working hours falls outside a member's professional obligations.
Treats an employer's view as determining whether the Standards have been breached.
hint: Ask what a member's conduct says about the qualities the profession depends on.
explanation: Standard I(D) prohibits conduct involving dishonesty, fraud or deceit, or any act that reflects adversely on a member's professional reputation, integrity or competence. A conviction for falsifying documents speaks directly to honesty, so it engages the Standard even though the dispute was personal and the employer took no action. Had the matter involved conduct with no bearing on honesty or trustworthiness, the Standard would not have been triggered.

stem: Ngo Thi Lan, CFA, disagrees strongly with a valuation published by a rival firm. On a public forum she writes that the rival's analysts are incompetent and that their clients are being deceived, without setting out any analysis to support the claim. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Lan most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because critical commentary on rival research is permitted
breached the Standards, because unsupported public attacks reflect poorly on her
acted appropriately, because she expressed an opinion rather than a factual claim
distractor_reason: Confuses reasoned professional criticism with an unsupported attack on competence.
Treats the label of opinion as removing responsibility for a damaging public assertion.
hint: Distinguish criticism supported by analysis from an assertion that simply disparages.
explanation: Standard I(D) covers conduct that reflects adversely on a member's professional reputation, integrity or competence, which includes making unsupported public allegations of incompetence and deception. Vigorous disagreement with a rival's valuation is legitimate when it rests on stated analysis; asserting deception without any is not. Had Lan published a reasoned critique of the valuation methodology, the Standard would not have been engaged.

stem: Truong Van Kien, CFA, an analyst in Ho Chi Minh City, interviews a listed retailer's logistics contractor and a sample of its suppliers. Combining their answers with public filings, he concludes that the retailer's quarterly revenue will fall well short of guidance. None of the parties gave him confidential information. Kien publishes the conclusion. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Kien most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because the conclusion is material and not yet public
acted appropriately, because the conclusion came from non-material public pieces
breached the Standards, because the suppliers were not authorised to speak with him
distractor_reason: Treats the materiality of a conclusion as making its underlying research improper.
Introduces an authorisation requirement that the Standard does not impose on third parties.
hint: Ask whether the material element came from the sources or from the analyst's own work.
explanation: Standard II(A) prohibits acting on material nonpublic information, but the mosaic approach permits an analyst to reach a material conclusion by combining public information with non-material pieces gathered from diligent research. Because no source supplied material nonpublic information, the value lies in Kien's own analysis and publication is permitted. Had a company insider told him the revenue figure directly, the Standard would have been breached. Standard V(A) supports the conclusion by requiring a reasonable and adequate basis.

stem: Sim Hui Xian, CFA, works in the corporate advisory division of a Singapore bank and learns that a client will announce a large acquisition in ten days. She does not trade. At a family dinner she mentions that a relative's holding in the target may soon do well. The relative buys more shares the next morning. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Sim most likely:
options: did not breach, because she took no position in the target company herself
did not breach, because a remark at a private dinner is not a market communication
breached the Standards, because she caused another to act on the information
distractor_reason: Assumes the prohibition bites at trading rather than at conveying the information.
Treats a private setting as placing a disclosure outside the reach of the Standard.
hint: Consider the full range of conduct the prohibition covers beyond dealing for oneself.
explanation: Standard II(A) prohibits members who possess material nonpublic information from acting on it and from causing others to act on it, so tipping is caught even where the member trades nothing. A hint sufficient to prompt a relative's purchase conveys the substance of the information, and the private setting is immaterial. Had Sim said nothing until the announcement was public, no breach would have occurred. Standard III(E) is also engaged by the disclosure of client information.

stem: Kieu Minh Tam, CFA, is added to a deal team and comes into possession of nonpublic information about a pending transaction. He asks how his firm should manage the risk that the information reaches colleagues who trade. Under the CFA Institute Code and Standards, the recommended procedure is most likely to:
options: restrict the information within the deal team using an information barrier
suspend all trading by the firm in the affected security until announcement
record the information in a central register accessible to research staff
distractor_reason: Treats a firm-wide trading halt as the recommended control rather than a targeted barrier.
Confuses controlling access to sensitive information with circulating it internally.
hint: Consider the control designed to keep sensitive information from spreading across a firm.
explanation: Standard II(A) recommends that firms adopt information barriers to limit the flow of material nonpublic information to those with a need to know, so that other parts of the firm may continue to operate. Blanket trading suspensions are not the recommended approach, and recording the information where research staff can see it would spread rather than contain it. Restricted lists and watch lists may supplement the barrier where a firm has a legitimate need to monitor activity.

stem: Cao Duy Khanh, CFA, manages a small-capitalisation fund. In the final hour of each quarter he places a series of buy orders in three thinly traded holdings, lifting their closing prices. He records the trades as portfolio rebalancing and reports the resulting quarter-end valuations to investors. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Khanh most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the purchases were genuine trades at market prices
breached the Standards, because the trades were placed to affect reported valuations
acted appropriately, because rebalancing at period end is ordinary portfolio practice
distractor_reason: Treats the reality of the transactions as answering the question of why they were placed.
Uses a routine label for the activity in place of examining its actual purpose.
hint: Look at the purpose behind the orders rather than at whether the trades were real.
explanation: Standard II(B) prohibits transactions intended to distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the aim of misleading market participants. Buying illiquid holdings into the close so that quarter-end valuations rise is transaction-based manipulation, and the trades being genuine does not change that purpose. Had the purchases followed from a rebalancing decision made independently of the reporting date, they would have been legitimate. Standard III(D) is also engaged by the performance figures reported to investors.

stem: Wee Chin Hock, CFA, runs a long position in a mid-cap manufacturer. He publishes a detailed note setting out his bullish view, discloses his position clearly, and presents his assumptions and their basis. The note attracts buying and the price rises, after which he sells part of his holding. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Wee most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the note disclosed his position and stated its reasoning
breached the Standards, because he sold into the demand his own note generated
breached the Standards, because publishing research on a personal holding misleads readers
distractor_reason: Treats a subsequent sale as evidence that the publication was intended to mislead.
Assumes holding a position in a covered security is itself a form of manipulation.
hint: Ask whether anything the member communicated to the market was false or concealed.
explanation: Standard II(B) addresses the dissemination of false or misleading information intended to mislead market participants; it does not prohibit publishing an honestly held view on a security the member owns. Because Wee disclosed his position and set out his reasoning, readers could weigh the note knowing his interest, and a later sale does not convert accurate analysis into manipulation. Had he concealed the holding or overstated his conviction to attract buyers, the Standard would have been breached. Standard VI(A) is satisfied by the disclosure made.

stem: Uong Thanh Son, CFA, posts on a widely followed forum that a listed developer has secured a major state contract. He has no basis for the statement and hopes the post will lift the share price ahead of his planned sale. The price rises and he sells. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Son most likely:
options: did not breach, because forum posts are opinion rather than formal published research
breached the Standards, because he spread false information to move the price
did not breach, because he traded at prices the market itself had set
distractor_reason: Treats the informality of the channel as removing responsibility for a false statement.
Uses the existence of a market price to excuse the conduct that produced it.
hint: Consider what the member told the market and what he intended it to achieve.
explanation: Standard II(B) prohibits the dissemination of false or misleading information with the intent of distorting prices or misleading market participants. Posting a fabricated contract award in order to sell into the resulting rise is information-based manipulation, and the informal setting of the forum offers no protection. Had Son posted an honest assessment of the developer's prospects, no breach would have arisen. Standard I(C) is also engaged by the false statement itself.

stem: Tran Minh Duc, CFA, advises a discretionary client at a Hanoi securities firm. The client's investment policy statement records a low risk tolerance and a five-year horizon for a house purchase. Duc places thirty percent of the account in a leveraged commodity fund after reading a broker note describing strong momentum in the sector. The policy statement is unchanged. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Duc most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the sector note supplied a reasonable basis for the trade
breached the Standards, because the position conflicts with the recorded risk tolerance
acted appropriately, because thirty percent leaves the majority of the account unleveraged
distractor_reason: Treats a reasonable basis for the security itself as sufficient without testing it against the client's recorded constraints.
Assumes a position below half the portfolio cannot conflict with a documented low risk tolerance.
hint: Ask what the client's recorded objectives and constraints permit before any new exposure is added.
explanation: Standard III(C) requires a member to judge the suitability of an investment against the client's written objectives, constraints and risk tolerance before acting. A leveraged commodity position is inconsistent with a recorded low risk tolerance and a five-year horizon for a specific spending need, so the allocation breaches the Standard. Had Duc first discussed the change with the client and revised the policy statement to reflect a higher risk tolerance, the position could have been appropriate. Standard V(A) would also be engaged if a single broker note were the only basis for the decision.

stem: Le Thanh Ha, CFA, manages a separately managed account for a client whose written policy statement limits foreign currency exposure to ten percent. During a telephone call the client says he is comfortable with more overseas exposure and asks Ha to use her judgement. Ha raises the foreign currency allocation to twenty-five percent and writes a note of the call in the client file. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Ha most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the client gave permission during the recorded call
breached the Standards, because the policy statement was not revised beforehand
acted appropriately, because her file note records the client's revised instruction
distractor_reason: Treats spoken permission as equivalent to a revision of the client's written constraints.
Assumes documenting a conversation satisfies the requirement to update the policy statement itself.
hint: Consider what must change in the client's documented constraints before a limit can be exceeded.
explanation: Standard III(C) requires a member to update a client's written policy statement when circumstances or objectives change, and to act within the constraints it records. A remark on a call expressing comfort with more exposure is not a revision of a documented limit, so raising the allocation to twenty-five percent breaches the Standard even though the call was noted. Had Ha obtained the client's agreement and amended the written limit before trading, the higher allocation would have been permissible. The requirement is that the constraint be revised, not merely that the conversation be recorded.

stem: Pornchai Suwan, CFA, opens a discretionary account for a new client at a Bangkok asset management company. The client transfers funds and asks that the money be put to work quickly, since markets look attractive. Suwan begins building an equity portfolio the same week. A written statement of the client's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance is scheduled to be prepared the following month. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Suwan most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because investing began before the objectives were recorded
acted appropriately, because the client asked for prompt investment of the funds
acted appropriately, because the written statement was scheduled for the following month
distractor_reason: Treats a client's wish for speed as a substitute for establishing suitability first.
Assumes a planned future document can support investment decisions already taken.
hint: Consider what must exist before a discretionary account can be invested at all.
explanation: Standard III(C) requires a member to make a reasonable inquiry into a client's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance, and to record them in a written policy statement, before making a recommendation or taking investment action. Building the portfolio before that statement exists means the suitability of every holding is untested, so Suwan breaches the Standard. Had the statement been completed first, investing promptly at the client's request would have been appropriate. Client urgency does not shorten the inquiry that the Standard requires.

stem: Vo Quoc Bao, CFA, advises a private wealth client in Ho Chi Minh City whose policy statement seeks steady income at moderate risk. The client's existing holdings are concentrated in residential property. Bao adds a bond issued by a property developer, noting that the instrument carries an investment-grade domestic rating and pays a coupon consistent with the income objective. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Bao most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the rating and the coupon match the stated income objective
acted appropriately, because a rated bond carries less risk than direct property
breached the Standards, because the holding deepens an existing property concentration
distractor_reason: Judges the instrument on its own characteristics rather than against the portfolio as a whole.
Assumes a lower-risk security cannot worsen a risk already present across the account.
hint: Consider the level at which the suitability of a new holding has to be assessed.
explanation: Standard III(C) requires a member to judge the suitability of an investment in the context of the client's total portfolio, not in isolation. A property developer bond adds exposure to the same sector that already dominates the client's holdings, so it raises concentration risk beyond a moderate-risk mandate even though its rating and coupon look consistent with the income objective. Had the client's existing holdings been diversified across sectors, the same bond could have been suitable. Standard V(B) would also be engaged if the concentration effect were not communicated to the client.

stem: Dang Kim Chi, CFA, manages a public equity fund whose prospectus states a growth mandate with high volatility. A large unitholder approaching retirement tells Chi that the fund no longer suits her circumstances and asks her to hold more short-duration bonds. Chi shifts a portion of the fund into bonds so that the unitholder's needs are met. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Chi most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because the fund must be managed to its stated mandate
acted appropriately, because suitability is owed to the individual unitholder
acted appropriately, because the change lowers portfolio risk for a retiring investor
distractor_reason: Applies the individual suitability test to a pooled vehicle managed to a published mandate.
Assumes a reduction in risk is permissible whenever it benefits one investor in the fund.
hint: Consider what a pooled fund's published strategy commits the manager to, and to whom that commitment runs.
explanation: Where a member manages a pooled vehicle to a stated mandate, Standard III(C) requires investment actions to be consistent with the objectives and constraints of that portfolio rather than with the circumstances of any individual investor. Shifting the fund toward bonds departs from the published growth mandate and disadvantages the unitholders who bought that strategy, so Chi breaches the Standard. Had Chi instead advised the unitholder that the fund no longer matched her circumstances and left the mandate intact, the Standard would have been satisfied. Standard III(B) is also engaged, since the change favours one investor over the rest of the unitholders.

stem: Phan Gia Linh, CFA, manages assets for a corporate pension plan. The company's finance director, who appointed her, asks that the portfolio be tilted toward bonds issued by the company's main customers, arguing that this would strengthen a commercial relationship the company values. Linh implements the tilt. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Linh most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the finance director is the client who appointed her
acted appropriately, because the tilt serves the sponsoring company's wider interests
breached the Standards, because the plan beneficiaries are the client she serves
distractor_reason: Confuses the person who hires the manager with the party to whom loyalty is owed.
Allows a benefit to the plan sponsor to displace the interests of the beneficiaries.
hint: For a pension plan, ask whose interests the manager is there to serve.
explanation: Standard III(A) requires a member managing a pension plan to act for the benefit of the plan participants and beneficiaries, not for the plan sponsor or the individual who awarded the mandate. Tilting the portfolio to support a commercial relationship of the sponsoring company subordinates the beneficiaries' interests, so the Standard is breached. Had the bonds been selected on their investment merits within the plan's mandate, the allocation would have been proper.

stem: Koh Wei Sheng, CFA, directs the trading of a client portfolio to a broker whose execution costs are somewhat higher than a rival's, because that broker supplies research his team uses in managing the same portfolio. He documents the arrangement and reviews execution quality each quarter. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Koh most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because a costlier broker cannot be chosen for a client
acted appropriately, because the research supports management of that same portfolio
breached the Standards, because directing trades for research disadvantages the client
distractor_reason: Treats cost as the sole criterion, ignoring the value the client receives in return.
Assumes any research arrangement conflicts with the duty owed to the client.
hint: Ask who receives the benefit purchased with the client's commission.
explanation: Standard III(A) permits a member to use client brokerage to obtain research that benefits that client, provided the arrangement is disclosed, documented and monitored, since the commission then buys value the client actually receives. Koh's documentation and quarterly execution review are the procedures the Standard contemplates. Had the research been used for other portfolios or for the firm's own account, using this client's commission would have breached the duty of loyalty.

stem: Dinh Hoang Nam, CFA, holds proxy voting authority for several client portfolios. To reduce administrative cost he adopts a policy of voting with management on all resolutions, without reviewing the agenda of any meeting. He records the policy in his files. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Nam most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because voting requires care informed by client interest
acted appropriately, because a documented voting policy discharges the duty
acted appropriately, because routine resolutions rarely affect the value of a holding
distractor_reason: Treats the existence of a policy as a substitute for the judgement the policy should guide.
Assumes the typical case can settle in advance how every resolution should be voted.
hint: Consider whether voting rights are part of the client's asset or an administrative chore.
explanation: Standard III(A) treats proxy voting as part of the prudent management of client assets, so votes must be cast with care and in the client's interest rather than on an unexamined default. A blanket policy of supporting management without reviewing any agenda abandons that judgement, so the Standard is breached. Had Nam adopted a cost-effective policy that still identified and reviewed resolutions capable of affecting value, he would have complied.

stem: Yeo Li Ping, CFA, manages an equity fund and also serves without pay on the board of a charity. The charity asks her to place its endowment with a manager who has offered it a fee discount, and she agrees. That manager runs a competing fund. She makes no disclosure to her employer. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Yeo most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because the unpaid role was not disclosed to her employer
acted appropriately, because the charity role is unpaid and outside work
acted appropriately, because the endowment obtained better terms through her decision
distractor_reason: Treats the absence of payment as removing an outside role from a member's obligations.
Uses a favourable outcome for one party to answer a question about competing duties.
hint: Ask what a member owes an employer when an outside role touches the same market.
explanation: Standard IV(A) requires disclosure of outside activities that could create a conflict with the employer's interests, and Standard III(A) requires undivided loyalty in each fiduciary role a member holds. Directing an endowment to a competing manager while serving her employer, without any disclosure, places the two duties in unresolved conflict. Had Yeo disclosed the trusteeship and recused herself from the manager selection, both duties could have been met. The absence of a fee does not lessen the obligation.

stem: Ta Bich Ngoc, CFA, is publishing a recommendation change on a listed bank. Her firm's policy is to release research to all clients at the same time. Before the release she telephones two large institutional clients to preview the change, reasoning that they hold the largest positions and face the greatest risk. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Ngoc most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because larger holders face greater risk from the change
breached the Standards, because some clients received the change early
acted appropriately, because the two clients received a brief early summary
distractor_reason: Uses the size of a client's position to justify unequal access to a recommendation.
Treats a preview as materially different from the recommendation it discloses.
hint: Consider what fair dealing requires about the sequence in which clients learn of a change.
explanation: Standard III(B) requires members to deal fairly with all clients when disseminating investment recommendations, which means clients should have a fair opportunity to act on a change at broadly the same time. Previewing the change for two clients gives them an advantage over everyone else, and the size of their holdings does not justify it. Had Ngoc released the recommendation simultaneously and then discussed its implications with clients who called, the Standard would have been met.

stem: Trinh Van Hieu, CFA, receives a small allocation in an oversubscribed new issue. He distributes it pro rata among the client portfolios for which the issue is suitable, including two accounts that pay lower fees. His firm's premium service clients complain that they received the same proportionate treatment as everyone else. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Hieu most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because premium clients are entitled to priority allocation
breached the Standards, because low-fee accounts should not receive new issues
acted appropriately, because pro rata allocation among suitable accounts is fair
distractor_reason: Converts a difference in service level into a right to preference in allocations.
Assumes fee level rather than suitability should determine access to an offering.
hint: Ask what fair dealing measures allocation against when supply is limited.
explanation: Standard III(B) requires fair treatment of clients in the allocation of limited offerings, and pro rata allocation among the accounts for which the issue is suitable is the approach the Standard contemplates. Differences in service level may justify different levels of contact or reporting, but they do not create a right to preference in a scarce allocation. Had Hieu allocated first to premium clients and distributed only the remainder, the Standard would have been breached.

stem: Lam Tuan Kiet, CFA, offers two service levels. Clients paying a premium fee receive monthly commentary and quarterly meetings; standard clients receive quarterly commentary. Investment recommendations and changes are released to both groups at the same time, and the difference in service is described in the client agreement. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Lam most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because differentiated service disadvantages standard clients
acted appropriately, because the difference lies in service, not recommendations
breached the Standards, because commentary frequency shapes how advice is used
distractor_reason: Treats any difference between client tiers as inconsistent with fair dealing.
Assumes a disclosed difference in reporting frequency amounts to unequal access to advice.
hint: Distinguish the level of service a client buys from access to the recommendations themselves.
explanation: Standard III(B) permits members to offer different levels of service, provided the differences are disclosed and do not disadvantage any client in access to investment recommendations or actions. Because recommendations reach both groups simultaneously and the service difference is set out in the client agreement, the arrangement is consistent with the Standard. Had premium clients received recommendation changes before standard clients, fair dealing would have been breached.

stem: Quach Minh Duong, CFA, markets a new absolute return strategy. His presentation shows a five-year record, of which the first three years are simulated results produced by applying the strategy's rules to historical data. The chart is labelled as strategy performance and no distinction is drawn between the periods. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Duong most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because simulated results are shown as if actually achieved
acted appropriately, because the same rules were applied to the history
acted appropriately, because a longer record helps clients assess the strategy properly
distractor_reason: Treats methodological consistency as making back-tested results equivalent to real ones.
Uses the informational value of a longer record to excuse how that record is labelled.
hint: Consider what a reader assumes when a performance chart carries no qualification.
explanation: Standard III(D) requires performance information to be fair, accurate and complete, which means simulated or back-tested results must be clearly identified as such. Presenting three years of modelled results alongside two actual years under a single label leads clients to believe money was managed to those returns. Had the chart separated and labelled the back-tested period, the presentation would have complied. Standard I(C) is also engaged by the misleading impression created.

stem: Doan Khanh Ha, CFA, prepares marketing material for a balanced fund. She reports the fund's three best calendar years, which she selects because they demonstrate what the strategy can achieve, and omits the remaining four years of the fund's life. The years shown are accurately calculated. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Ha most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because the returns presented are accurately calculated figures
acted appropriately, because the selected years illustrate the strategy's real potential
breached the Standards, because selecting favourable years makes the record incomplete
distractor_reason: Treats arithmetical accuracy as sufficient when the selection itself distorts the picture.
Confuses what a strategy can achieve at its best with what it has actually delivered.
hint: Ask whether a set of true figures can still leave a reader with a false impression.
explanation: Standard III(D) requires performance presentation to be fair, accurate and complete, so a record cannot be assembled from the periods that flatter the strategy. Each figure being correctly calculated does not cure the distortion created by omitting four years, and readers will infer that the years shown are representative. Had Ha presented the full seven-year record, the material would have complied.

stem: Mai Thu Trang, CFA, receives a written request from a securities regulator conducting a formal investigation into a former client. The request covers account records that Trang holds. Her firm's client agreement promises that client information will be kept confidential. Trang provides the records to the regulator. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Trang most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because the agreement promised continuing confidentiality
acted appropriately, because a lawful regulatory demand overrides the duty
breached the Standards, because the duty survives the end of the relationship
distractor_reason: Treats a contractual confidentiality promise as displacing a lawful regulatory demand.
Correctly identifies that the duty survives, but overlooks the exception that applies here.
hint: Consider the situations in which the duty of confidentiality gives way.
explanation: Standard III(E) requires members to preserve the confidentiality of current, former and prospective client information, but the duty does not apply where disclosure is required by law, including in response to a lawful regulatory investigation. Providing the records to the regulator therefore falls within the exception, even though the duty otherwise survives the end of the relationship. Had a competitor or journalist made the same request, disclosure would have breached the Standard.

stem: Chu Nhat Minh, CFA, moves to a new firm. Wanting to demonstrate his experience, he shows his new colleagues an anonymised file from his former employer containing a client's portfolio structure and investment objectives. He removes the client's name but leaves the other details intact. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Minh most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because removing the name protects the client's identity fully
breached the Standards, because he disclosed information about a former client
acted appropriately, because the information relates to a relationship that has ended
distractor_reason: Assumes anonymisation is complete when identifying detail remains in the record.
Treats the end of a client relationship as ending the obligation of confidentiality.
hint: Ask how long the obligation lasts and how much detail makes a client identifiable.
explanation: Standard III(E) requires confidentiality to be preserved for former clients as well as current ones, and a portfolio structure with stated objectives may identify a client even without a name attached. Sharing the file to demonstrate his experience serves Minh's interests rather than the client's, so the Standard is breached. Had he described his experience in general terms without reproducing client records, he would have complied. Standard IV(A) is also engaged by his use of a former employer's records.

stem: Duong Khac Vinh, CFA, has accepted an offer from a rival firm but has not yet resigned. During his notice period he prepares marketing material describing the strategy he will run at the new firm, using his own laptop outside office hours. He takes no client list or research file with him. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Vinh most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because he used personal time and took no employer property
breached the Standards, because preparing to compete while employed is prohibited
breached the Standards, because his notice period had not yet come to an end
distractor_reason: Treats all preparation for a future role as inconsistent with the duty of loyalty.
Assumes the formal end of employment is the line rather than the use of employer resources.
hint: Distinguish preparing to compete from actually competing while still employed.
explanation: Standard IV(A) permits a departing employee to make preparations to begin a competing enterprise, provided the preparations do not breach the duty of loyalty by using employer property or soliciting clients while still employed. Working on his own equipment in his own time and taking no records keeps Vinh within that boundary. Had he copied a client list or approached clients before resigning, the Standard would have been breached.

stem: Ho Thi Kim Ngan, CFA, resigns from a Hanoi asset manager. Before leaving she emails herself a spreadsheet of the valuation models she built during her employment, reasoning that the models reflect her own analytical work and that she will need them in her next role. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Ngan most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because she personally built the models during her employment
breached the Standards, because work made for an employer belongs to it
acted appropriately, because the models contain no client or confidential information
distractor_reason: Confuses authorship of work product with ownership of it.
Treats the absence of client data as settling the question of who owns the file.
hint: Ask who owns material created in the course of employment, and who must consent to its removal.
explanation: Standard IV(A) requires members not to deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities or to misappropriate property, and models built in the course of employment are the employer's work product. Taking them without written permission breaches the Standard regardless of who did the analytical work or whether client data is present. Had Ngan obtained the employer's written consent before leaving, she could have used the models elsewhere.

stem: Toh Kai Ming, CFA, is instructed by his employer to market a structured product to retail clients using a brochure that overstates the level of principal protection. He raises the point with compliance, which confirms the wording will not change. He continues to distribute the brochure while looking for another role. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Toh most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because loyalty requires him to follow his employer's instruction
acted appropriately, because he escalated the concern to the compliance department
breached the Standards, because he continued distributing material he knows misleads
distractor_reason: Treats the duty of loyalty as extending to instructions that would breach other duties.
Assumes raising a concern internally discharges the duty when the conduct continues.
hint: Consider what a member must do when an employer's instruction cannot lawfully be followed.
explanation: Standard IV(A) does not require obedience to an instruction that would cause a member to breach the Code and Standards, and Standard I(C) prohibits knowingly distributing misleading material. Once compliance declined to change the wording, continuing to distribute the brochure makes Toh a participant in the misrepresentation. Had he refused to distribute the brochure and dissociated from the activity, he would have complied. Looking for another role does not answer the obligation in the meantime.

stem: Ngamdee Suchart, CFA, manages a portfolio for a family office. The family principal offers him the use of a holiday apartment each year if returns exceed a stated benchmark. Suchart tells two colleagues about the offer over lunch and accepts it. He makes no written disclosure to his employer. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Suchart most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because colleagues at the firm were informed of the arrangement
acted appropriately, because the benefit is contingent on the client's own results
breached the Standards, because written consent from his employer was not obtained
distractor_reason: Treats informal mention to colleagues as satisfying a requirement of written consent.
Assumes a performance-linked benefit falls outside the additional compensation rules.
hint: Consider the form the employer's agreement has to take before such an offer may be accepted.
explanation: Standard IV(B) prohibits members from accepting compensation or benefits from a party other than their employer that compete with or might create a conflict with the employer's interest, unless written consent is obtained from all parties involved. A holiday apartment conditional on performance is exactly such a benefit, and a conversation with colleagues is not consent from the employer. Had Suchart obtained written consent setting out the terms and duration, acceptance would have been permitted.

stem: Luong Bao Tram, CFA, is offered a consulting fee by a company she covers as an analyst, in exchange for advising its board on capital structure. She informs her employer in writing, sets out the fee and the expected time commitment, and obtains written approval before starting. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Tram most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because an analyst cannot take fees from a covered company
acted appropriately, because she obtained written consent to the arrangement
breached the Standards, because the fee creates a conflict that consent cannot resolve
distractor_reason: Reads the Standard as an outright prohibition rather than a consent requirement.
Assumes a conflict of this kind lies beyond what disclosure and consent can address.
hint: Ask whether the Standard forbids the arrangement or regulates how it may be entered into.
explanation: Standard IV(B) does not prohibit outside compensation; it requires written consent from all parties after full disclosure of the terms, including amount and duration. Tram's written notification and prior approval meet that requirement. Had she started the consulting work before approval, or disclosed only the existence of the fee without its terms, the Standard would have been breached. Standard VI(A) separately requires disclosure of the conflict to investors relying on her research.

stem: Ong Siew Peng, CFA, heads a trading desk. Her firm has no procedure for reviewing personal trading by desk staff, and she has raised this with senior management twice without result. She continues supervising the desk. A junior trader is later found to have front-run client orders. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Ong most likely:
options: did not breach, because she raised the deficiency with senior management twice
breached the Standards, because she supervised without adequate procedures
did not breach, because responsibility for firm procedures rests above her
distractor_reason: Treats escalation as discharging the duty when the supervisor keeps accepting the role.
Transfers a supervisor's personal obligation upward on the basis of the reporting line.
hint: Consider what a supervisor must do when the firm will not give her the tools to supervise.
explanation: Standard IV(C) requires members with supervisory responsibility to make reasonable efforts to detect and prevent violations, and a member who cannot discharge that duty must decline supervisory responsibility in writing until adequate procedures are adopted. Raising the gap twice and then continuing to supervise leaves Ong accountable for the failure that follows. Had she declined the supervisory role in writing pending proper procedures, she would have complied.

stem: Vu Anh Tuan, CFA, supervises four analysts. His firm maintains a detailed compliance manual and a personal trading pre-clearance system, and Tuan enforces both. One analyst nonetheless conceals a personal holding by trading through a relative's account. The concealment is discovered by the pre-clearance review. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Tuan most likely:
options: did not breach, because reasonable procedures were in place and enforced
breached the Standards, because a violation occurred among the staff he supervises
breached the Standards, because the concealment went undetected
distractor_reason: Treats supervisory responsibility as strict liability for any subordinate's misconduct.
Measures compliance by whether detection was immediate rather than whether it was reasonable.
hint: Ask what standard a supervisor's efforts are measured against.
explanation: Standard IV(C) requires reasonable efforts to detect and prevent violations, not a guarantee that none will occur. Where an adequate compliance system exists, is enforced, and in fact uncovers the concealment, the supervisor has met the Standard even though a subordinate broke the rules. Had Tuan known of warning signs and failed to investigate, or allowed the system to go unenforced, the conclusion would differ.

stem: Thai Ngoc Bich, CFA, learns that an analyst she supervises may have shared draft research with a favoured client. She reminds the whole team of the firm's policy at the next meeting but takes no further step, and does not restrict the analyst's contact with clients while the matter is unresolved. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Bich most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because a general reminder is an inadequate response
did not breach, because she promptly raised the policy with the whole team again
did not breach, because the allegation was not established as fact
distractor_reason: Treats a broad restatement of policy as an investigation of a specific suspected breach.
Assumes a supervisor need not act until suspected misconduct has been proved.
hint: Consider what a supervisor must do once a specific concern about one person arises.
explanation: Standard IV(C) requires a supervisor who learns of possible misconduct to initiate an investigation and to take steps to prevent further violations while it proceeds. A general reminder to the team neither establishes what happened nor limits the risk, so the response falls short. Had Bich escalated the matter, launched an inquiry and placed appropriate limits on the analyst's client contact in the meantime, the Standard would have been satisfied.

stem: Kwok Ka Yan, CFA, issues a buy recommendation on a regional airline after reading a favourable note from a broker she considers reliable. She does not examine the broker's assumptions or test them against the airline's filings, and her own note repeats the broker's earnings forecast. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Kwok most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because she relied on a source she considers reliable
breached the Standards, because she established no reasonable basis herself
acted appropriately, because third-party research may be used in forming a view
distractor_reason: Treats a source's reputation as a substitute for the member's own diligence.
Confuses the permissibility of using third-party research with reliance on it untested.
hint: Ask what work the member herself must do before putting her name to a recommendation.
explanation: Standard V(A) requires members to exercise diligence and to have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any recommendation they make. Third-party research may be used, but the member must make reasonable efforts to satisfy herself that its assumptions and methods are sound. Had Kwok reviewed the broker's assumptions against the airline's filings and formed her own view, the Standard would have been met.

stem: Sirikul Anong, CFA, evaluates an external quantitative model her firm plans to use in constructing portfolios. She reviews its inputs and assumptions, tests it against historical periods including two market shocks, and documents the limitations she identifies. She then recommends its use with those limitations noted. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Anong most likely:
options: breached the Standards, because a model built outside the firm is unreliable
breached the Standards, because historical testing proves nothing
acted appropriately, because she tested the model and noted its limits
distractor_reason: Reads the Standard as excluding externally developed tools rather than requiring their review.
Treats testing against history as incapable of contributing to a reasonable basis.
hint: Consider what diligence looks like when the analytical tool comes from outside the firm.
explanation: Standard V(A) permits reliance on external models where the member makes reasonable efforts to understand their inputs, assumptions and limitations, and tests them appropriately. Anong's review, stress testing and documentation of limitations are precisely what the Standard contemplates. Had she adopted the model without examining its assumptions or testing it, she would have lacked a reasonable basis.

stem: Cheung Ho Yin, CFA, faces a client deadline and issues a recommendation on a newly listed company after reviewing only its prospectus, without the site visit and supplier interviews his firm's process requires. He notes in the report that his work was limited by time. According to the CFA Institute Code and Standards, Cheung most likely:
options: acted appropriately, because he disclosed the limits of his work
